resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
The word "now" in the original textbook refers to the period when it was written.
In the book's comparison, the Soviet Union then produced nearly five times as much electricity in a single day as it had in the whole of 1921, which the book identifies as the first year of implementing the nationwide electrification plan.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
In the figures reported by the original textbook for its own period, hydroelectric stations supplied about $20\%$ of the Soviet Union's total electricity.
The book describes the Krasnoyarsk Hydroelectric Power Station as named for the anniversary marking 50 years since the founding of the Soviet Union, and calls it the world's largest hydroelectric station at that time.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
It also describes the station's hydroelectric generating units as the world's most powerful at that time, giving their power as 500000 kilowatts.
The book gives the station's total power as six million kilowatts.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
The original textbook describes a trend toward higher-power thermal power stations.
According to its figures for that period, large numbers of thermal stations in the Soviet Union each had a power of more than one million kilowatts, and many exceeded two million kilowatts.
It gives the power of the Krivorozhsk Thermal Power Station as three million kilowatts and describes it as the world's largest thermal power station at that time.

resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
The original textbook describes a unified all-Soviet power system then taking shape by connecting the power systems of Siberia and Central Asia with those of the European part of the Soviet Union.
It explains that these connections improved the reliability and flexibility of electricity supply across the country's vast territory.
According to the textbook, this task required the construction of transmission trunk lines operating at 500000 volts, 750000 volts, and 1150000 volts.
